beats.text: Think about who you were ten years ago. Different person, right?
Now think ten years ahead. You'll stay pretty much the same. Right?
Researchers asked over nineteen thousand people, aged eighteen to sixty-eight.
At every age, people said they had changed a lot. And predicted they would change very little.
Psychologists call it the end of history illusion.
People would pay about eighty dollars to see their favorite band from ten years ago. But about a hundred and twenty-nine to see today's favorite, ten years from now.
As one researcher put it: at every age, we think we're having the last laugh. And at every age, we're wrong.
So the person you are right now? Not the final version.

sources: Quoidbach, Gilbert & Wilson (2013). The end of history illusion. Science 339(6115). Six studies, >19,000 participants aged 18-68: people reported more change over the past decade than they predicted for the next decade, at every age.

NYT (Tierney, 3 Jan 2013): typical willingness to pay $80 to see the favorite band from a decade ago now vs $129 to see the current favorite in ten years; Gilbert quote 'At every age we think we're having the last laugh, and at every age we're wrong.'
Caveat: cross-sectional design; critics question memory reliability.
